## The Lithosphere and Plate Driving Forces
Why it matters: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, so mapping quakes maps the plates.
Try first: before reading on, write down what the lithosphere is made of and what lies beneath it.
The lithosphere is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates. These plates float on the ductile asthenosphere, a layer that flows slowly.
The plates themselves stay rigid; the layer beneath them flows, and that flow permits motion.
Takeaway: rigid plates ride on a flowing layer beneath them.
Quick check: type the name of the layer beneath the plates.
Try first: attempt to list three mechanisms that drive plate motion before reading the answer.
Plates move because of mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push. Relative motion between plates is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Takeaway: three drivers — mantle convection, slab pull, ridge push — with rates in cm yr⁻¹.
Quick check: type the unit used for relative plate motion.
Try first: from memory, sketch which boundary type you think produces the deepest earthquakes, then compare with the table below.
Boundary types map onto fault styles and depths:
- Divergent → plates pull apart → normal-fault earthquakes, shallow depths
- Convergent → plates collide → thrust-fault earthquakes, deep to shallow
- Transform → plates slide past → strike-slip earthquakes, shallow to intermediate
Takeaway: each boundary type has its own fault style and depth range.
Quick check: type the fault style typical of transform boundaries.
Try first: propose your own explanation for why earthquakes cluster at boundaries before reading the four mechanisms.
Four mechanisms explain the clustering:
1. Stress accumulation — plate edges are locked by friction; strain builds until it exceeds rock strength.
2. Fault geometry — pre-existing faults concentrate slip.
3. Rheological contrast — cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation.
4. Geometric incompatibility — curved plate margins force localized shear zones.
Takeaway: clustering arises from stress accumulation, fault geometry, rheological contrast, and geometric incompatibility.
Quick check: type the mechanism in which friction locks plate edges.
Retrieval from earlier: type the three mechanisms that drive plate motion.
Watch out: a common wrong idea is that earthquakes occur anywhere equally often. The record shows clustering at plate boundaries, not random distribution.
Worked example: a strike-slip, shallow-to-intermediate earthquake implies a transform boundary, because transform plates slide past one another. Now do the same kind: a deep-to-shallow thrust-fault earthquake — type which boundary type it indicates and why.
Tomorrow, recall this one point: earthquakes trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, not a random distribution.
Key: Earthquakes trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, not random distribution.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Why it matters: earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions, so knowing the boundary types tells you where and how quakes occur.
